title: A pilot scorecard
scenario: You are head of shared services at a hotel group with 1,800 staff in 12 hotels. An AI assistant answers staff questions about leave, expenses and payroll. A pilot ran for eight weeks, and the board meets on Thursday. You must write the pilot scorecard. The exhibit holds what you know. All numbers are made up for this case.
exhibit:
BRIEF:
  The assistant ran at 6 hotels, drawn at random, for 8 weeks.
  The other 6 hotels worked as before.
  The board will decide: roll out, fix or stop.

TARGETS (written before the pilot):
  Correct answers: 92% or more
  Payroll answers: 99% or more

TEST SET (160 real questions from last year's HR inbox):
  Leave 70, expenses 60, payroll 30
  All are clear, one-sentence questions with every detail given.
  Correct: leave 66 of 70, expenses 56 of 60, payroll 27 of 30

HAND-OFF CHECK (a separate set):
  Rule: payroll disputes and harassment complaints go to a person.
  40 messages, all of these two kinds.
  Handed to a person: 40 of 40

TIME SAVED:
  Vendor claim: the assistant saves 6 minutes per question for HR staff.
  Pilot hotels: 5,000 questions a month answered by the assistant.
  40% of them would have gone to the HR team. Staff would have found the other 60% on the FAQ page.
  HR staff cost, loaded: $30 per hour.
  Saved HR time goes to the paperwork backlog, which now needs overtime.

HR HOURS ON ROUTINE QUESTIONS (against the weeks before):
  Pilot hotels: 31% lower
  Other hotels: 6% lower
  The pilot hotels also started a new online leave form in week 1. The other hotels did not.

questions.prompt: The 160 test questions are all clear and complete. What should the team add to the test set first?

options.text: More clear questions of the same kind, until the set reaches 1,000 questions in total.
options.explanation: A bigger set of easy questions is still an easy test. Anthropic's guide says to mirror real tasks and to add edge cases.

options.text: Only the ten questions that staff ask most often, so the test matches the most common use.
options.explanation: Common questions are already in the set. Real staff also send messy messages, and those are the ones the test misses.

options.text: Edge cases: missing details, very long messages, and cases where two HR experts disagree.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's guide lists edge cases to add: irrelevant or missing input, overly long input, and ambiguous cases where even humans would not agree.

options.text: Questions that the vendor writes, so that every answer is already known and has been checked.
options.explanation: The vendor's questions would not mirror your staff's real messages. The test should come from your own work, such as the HR inbox.

questions.prompt: The assistant sent 40 of 40 sensitive messages to a person. What does the hand-off check show?

options.text: Little yet, as no message in the set needs an answer, so it may hand off almost everything.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic's post says to test cases where a behaviour should happen and where it should not. A one-sided test can end with a tool that does it almost every time.

options.text: It is safe to launch, because a result of 100% means the hand-off rule works in every case we meet.
options.explanation: A perfect score on a one-sided set proves little. The set has no ordinary question to show that the assistant still answers.

options.text: The set is too small, because 40 messages cannot test a rule, so the check needs 400 messages.
options.explanation: Size is not the main gap. Even 400 sensitive messages would leave out the cases where the assistant should answer for itself.

options.text: It is a regression test, so a pass rate near 100% is expected and nothing else is needed.
options.explanation: Regression tests should pass nearly always, but this set is still missing the cases where no hand-off is right.

questions.prompt: Using the course's ROI sheet and the vendor's 6 minutes (labelled as a vendor claim), what monthly benefit from saved time can the scorecard show?

options.explanation: This counts all 5,000 questions. Only 40% of them would have reached the HR team, so the benefit is smaller.

options.text: About $6,000.
options.explanation: Right. 5,000 x 40% = 2,000 questions. 2,000 x 6 minutes = 12,000 minutes, and at $0.50 a minute that is $6,000. The time goes to paid backlog work, so it counts. The 6 minutes is a vendor claim, so label it and measure it.

options.text: About $9,000.
options.explanation: This uses the 60% that staff would have found on the FAQ page. That time was never an HR cost, so it is not a benefit.
This counts the 12,000 saved minutes as dollars. At $30 an hour each minute is worth $0.50.

questions.prompt: What can the board be told about the 31% drop in HR hours at the pilot hotels?

options.text: The assistant caused all of it, because drawing the hotels at random removes every other cause.
options.explanation: Random groups help, but the pilot hotels also got a new leave form. A random draw does not separate two changes made together.

options.text: The 6% drop at the other hotels shows the assistant has no effect, because hotels without it improved.
options.explanation: The gap between 31% and 6% is large. But it still mixes the assistant with the new leave form.

options.text: The form can be ignored, because a 25-point gap is too big for anything except the assistant.
options.explanation: The size of a gap does not show its cause. The form alone could explain a large share of a fall in leave questions.

options.text: Part of it may come from the leave form, so the pilot cannot show the assistant's own effect.
options.explanation: Right. The pilot should change one thing at a time. With two changes, the board cannot know which one caused the drop.

questions.prompt: Which opening line fits the board scorecard best?

options.text: This pilot ran for eight weeks at six of our twelve hotels in total, with 160 test questions and about 5,000 chats a month in the pilot hotels.
options.explanation: This is background. A report should start with the ask, then give the evidence, the risks and the next step.

options.text: Pilot results are positive: 93.1% overall accuracy and 31% fewer routine HR hours, so we ask for a full rollout at all hotels.
options.explanation: This hides the payroll miss at 90% against a 99% target. The 31% also mixes in the new leave form.

options.text: Ask: roll out for leave and expenses; keep payroll with staff and re-test it; leave measured 94% (66 of 70) and expenses 93% (56 of 60).
options.explanation: Right. It leads with the ask, gives labelled numbers with sample sizes, and fits the scope to the cost of a mistake. OpenAI's accuracy guide shows this middle path.

options.text: The vendor says staff love the assistant and that it saves 6 minutes a question, so we ask for a one-year contract now.
options.explanation: These are vendor claims, not measured pilot results. A scorecard should compare measured results with targets set before the pilot.
